title: Advanced execution
subtitle: State machines, unsafe boundaries, and evidence

lessons.title: A future is suspended work
lessons.task: Create an async future that increments counter once and returns its new value when polled.
lessons.hint: Return an async move block that captures the borrowed Cell.
body: Calling an async function constructs a future. Its body runs when polled, and values needed across suspension points become part of its state. Async does not automatically create a thread or accelerate CPU-bound work.

A future that returns Pending must arrange a wakeup when progress is possible. Executors poll ready tasks; blocking inside poll can stall other tasks sharing that executor. Production code normally uses await and a runtime.

Pin is an address-stability contract relevant to futures that may contain self-references. Box::pin is a convenient owning approach; not every future needs heap allocation. These exercises manually poll tiny futures only to reveal the protocol.

steps.title: Yield and request another poll
steps.task: Implement a future that returns Pending once, calls wake_by_ref, then returns Ready(7).
steps.hint: Use the bool as state. Set it before requesting the wakeup.
body: This toy future wakes immediately so it can be polled again. Real I/O futures register the task’s waker with an event source. Repeatedly waking without progress wastes CPU; do not turn this example into a busy-loop executor.

lessons.title: Make the proof explicit
lessons.task: Return None outside the slice; otherwise return a reference using get_unchecked after a bounds guard. Add a safety comment.
lessons.hint: Check index < xs.len() before entering the unsafe block.
lessons.concept: A safe interface around unsafe access
body: Unsafe permits operations whose safety the compiler cannot prove. It does not disable borrowing rules or make code inherently faster. Undefined behavior can invalidate the entire program’s assumptions.

A safe wrapper must validate every precondition for every caller. For get_unchecked the index must be in bounds even if the returned reference is never dereferenced. Tests can catch mistakes but cannot prove absence of undefined behavior.
The exercise is intentionally equivalent to slice::get. Prefer that safe method in real code unless profiling and generated-code inspection justify a carefully audited unsafe implementation.

lessons.title: Measure work before nanoseconds
lessons.task: Search sorted xs for target and return (found, comparisons), counting each midpoint comparison.
lessons.hint: Maintain a half-open [lo, hi) interval and halve it using the midpoint ordering.
body: Rust cannot rescue an unnecessarily quadratic algorithm. Counting operations can expose scaling without noisy wall-clock comparisons. A sorted slice supports binary search instead of scanning every element.

For real timing, use optimized builds, realistic inputs, warmup and repeated samples; keep setup outside the measured region. black_box can discourage some optimizations but is a best-effort hint, not a substitute for sound benchmark design.

The Playground runner uses debug mode on shared infrastructure. We check a logarithmic comparison budget here, not a timing threshold. Validate speed claims locally with release benchmarks and profile allocations, CPU time, and cache behavior as appropriate.
